**Ch 074 draft — scan**

The draft is generally clean. "The stranger waved his hand" — antecedent for "the stranger" is Mayhew, who has just been named in context; no problem. "Macey, the chief mate" — named with role appositive, fine. The cutting-spade pole handling is slightly compressed but parses. No structural failures found.

---

**Ch 076 draft — scan**

**Candidate 1:** Flask's dialogue line about Fedallah's tusk.

Draft: *"Did you ever notice how that tusk of his—a long tooth, carved somehow into a snake's head—is a sort of omen?"*

Source: *"Did you ever notice how that tusk of his is a sort of carved into a snake's head, Stubb?"* — followed by Stubb's reply about Fedallah being the devil.

The draft adds "a long tooth, carved somehow into a snake's head" as a gloss (actually an improvement), and then ends with "is a sort of omen?" — the source doesn't say "omen"; it just ends the question about the snake-carving, to which Stubb responds. But the draft's question still parses and conveys the same suspicion. Not a structural failure.

**Candidate 2:** Stubb's speech — logical sequence within compressed monologue.

Draft: *"The devil is a curious chap, and a wicked one. They say he went a sauntering into the old flag-ship once… 'Take him,' says the governor… But I never look at Fedallah at all; if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks, and no one by—look down there, Flask—Aye, will I!"*

In the source, Stubb first says "I never look at Fedallah at all; if ever I get a chance of a dark night…" *before* the flag-ship story. In the draft, the flag-ship story comes first, then the dark-night threat is appended as a non-sequitur after "I'll eat this whale in one mouthful." The compressed monologue stitches two passages together out of order, making "But I never look at Fedallah at all" a **broken pivot**: the "But" implies a contrast with something just said, but what was just said was the flag-ship anecdote, not the claim that Stubb looks at Fedallah. In the source the "But" is not present in this reordered position — the contrast was between "Sink him! I never look at him at all" and what follows. Here the "But I never look at Fedallah at all" is spliced after a different passage, creating an incoherent pivot.

Gate test: A reader would genuinely be confused — Stubb just told the flag-ship story and concluded with the cholera joke, then suddenly says "But I never look at Fedallah at all" as if contradicting something, but nothing in the immediately preceding draft text says he does look at Fedallah. It reads as one side of a missing two-sided structure.

**Candidate 3:** "Stubb, you boasted of giving Fedallah a sea-toss; if he's going to live for ever, what good will pitching him overboard do?"

In the source, this is Flask's line after a long exchange about Fedallah's age (the mainmast/hoops exchange), which established that Fedallah is immortally old. That exchange was cut. The phrase "if he's going to live for ever" now lacks its premise — the reader hasn't seen the immortality established in this chapter's draft dialogue (only Stubb's devil-talk, not the specific age question). However, Stubb did say "does the devil live for ever; who ever heard that the devil was dead?" in the source — but that exchange is also cut from the draft. Flask's compressed question assumes the reader knows Fedallah lives forever, which was established only in cut material.

Gate test: The draft has Stubb say "the devil lives for ever" implicitly through the devil-identification framework, and Flask's question "if he's going to live for ever" can be parsed as following from the devil=Fedallah thread. A competent reader can follow this. Not a structural failure — just less scaffolded.

**Candidate 4:** *"But Stubb, you boasted of giving Fedallah a sea-toss"* — Flask says Stubb "boasted" of this earlier in the conversation. In the source, Stubb said explicitly: *"if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks, and no one by; look down there, Flask—pointing into the sea…—Aye, will I!"* In the draft this threat appears in the immediately preceding paragraph (the reordered monologue), so Flask's "you boasted" does have an antecedent in the draft. Not a broken pivot.
